name: The Carpenter household
head: carpenter_philo

arrival.note: 'Arrived here in July, 1832' - month precision, stated twice by Andreas in two chapters. THE COMPILER'S 1832 LIST AGREES AND IS COARSER. Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 1 (1895), printed page 89 (claim bk_mose1_001) names this man among those who came through Chicago in 1832 and decided to remain. A YEAR AND NOT A MONTH, from an 1895 compilation, so it corroborates this field and does not move it. THE GRADE CEILING IS THE SOURCE'S AND NOT THIS FIELD'S. Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois (1895) is a compiler sixty years after the fact; every claim taken off it is transcription_mediated and none is scan_verified, so nothing drawn from it is graded above `inferred` (the rule T-1322 set for the settlers table, kept here). AND ONE SENTENCE IN THE SAME VOLUME NARROWS THE MONTH THIS FIELD ALREADY CARRIES. Printed pages 573-574 (claim bk_mose1_013): "a month after his arrival, on the 19th of August, 1832, he organized a Sunday school". Read on the book's own wording that closes the arrival to WITHIN THE MONTH BEFORE 19 AUGUST 1832, which is on or after about 19 July. Andreas has "Arrived here in July, 1832", and the two together put the coming in the LAST THIRTEEN DAYS OF JULY 1832. THE VALUE DOES NOT MOVE AND THE PRECISION DOES NOT SHARPEN: 1832-07-01 is where this project carries a month, the narrowing is an inference on a compiler's phrasing rather than a stated date, and sharpening `month` to a fortnight on the strength of "a month after" would be reading the book harder than it can bear. It is recorded because it is the finest thing the volume says about any arrival in this reading, and a later run with a dated source should find it already here.

origin.note: A BIRTHPLACE, WHICH IS NOT THE SAME CLAIM. The Calumet Club roll of 1879 gives “Mass.” as where this man was BORN; this field asks where the household came FROM, and a generation that moved west in stages frequently did not come from the state it was born in. It is carried as the best statement of origin the sources make about this household and not as a last residence.

occupation.note: 'The earliest pharmaceutist of Chicago was Philo Carpenter, who arrived here in July, 1832, shortly thereafter opening a variety and drug store on what is now known as Lake Street, near the eastern bank of the river; and subsequently removing to South Water Street' (Andreas, scan p. 955). He advertised drugs, medicines, oils, paints and dye-stuffs in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833, over copy dated 22 November.

persons.note: DOCUMENTED CONTEMPORANEOUSLY AND RETROSPECTIVELY, which almost nobody in this parcel is. He was one of the twenty-eight electors of 10 August 1833 and got one vote for trustee; he was one of the nine village citizens among the twenty-six founding members of the First Presbyterian Church on 26 June 1833, and one of its three first elders, and Andreas notes he was the only Presbyterian among them, the rest being Congregationalists. Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 132 (scan p. 281), 'an imperfect list of the denizens of the town in the fall of 1833, not before named' - a name, a trade and usually an arrival year, compiled fifty years after the fact. OLD SETTLERS, 1882 — CORROBORATION, NOT A NEW FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's fourth annual reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, held 18 May 1882, printed this man among the guests present as “Carpenter. Philo, 57 Ashland avenue, Chicago.” (Chicago Tribune, 19 May 1882). The club's criterion was residence in Chicago before 1 January 1840 and majority by then: the roster therefore corroborates a pre-1840 Chicago residence and says he was alive in 1882. It gives NO year of arrival, and the address it prints is where he lived in 1882, forty-seven years after the scene date — it is not an 1835 residence and is not read as one. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Carpenter, Philo” (poll_1833_006, line 27); Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Carpenter, Philo” (tax_1833_012, line 64); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Carpenter, Philo” (poll_1834_023, line 192). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Carpenter' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). OLD SETTLERS, 1879 — A DATE THIS MAN GAVE FOR HIMSELF, AND STILL NOT A FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's FIRST reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, 27 May 1879, printed its register in the proceedings (Early Chicago, Chicago, 1879, pages 84-90), and this man's entry reads “Carpenter, Philo, | 1832, | Mass. | 74 | Chicago.” — name, his own date of arrival, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address, in the register's five columns. The date of arrival is HIS RECOLLECTION, set down forty to sixty years after the event; the address is where he lived in 1879 and is never read as an 1835 residence. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Philo Carpenter” (f1839_v0360, printed page 43, ward 2, voting for John H. Kinzie). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Carpenter' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins P. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 4 times, as “CARPENTER PHILO”, “CARPENTER P”, 1833-10-22 to 1836-06-23: 1 federal land entry — SE sec 08 T39N R14E and 1 lot in the platted town — lot 7 of block 40 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L7BL40CHIOT, as printed) and 2 parcels of the school section — BL128 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL27 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read, 165.71 acres stated in all, for $3507.00 (ls0037, ls0127, ls0128, ls1026). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $3000.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: CARPENTER PHILO matches Philo Carpenter: the forename names Philo Carpenter of the 3 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE 1840 FEDERAL CENSUS — A HEAD FIVE YEARS AFTER THE SCENE, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1840 federal census of Chicago, read line by line off the left sheets in this repository, carries 1 head of this name — “Philo Carpenter” (33S7-9YYJ-RC, printed page 217, line 29). This project has ruled the head a MATCH for this person: the full name agrees, it is unique on both sides, and a discriminator independent of the name — directory persistence — separately places the same person in Chicago after the 1840 book was taken. Under the rule that decided it (L6 matched), by the crosswalk's own ladder (data/research/census_1840/resident_crosswalk.json). LATER EVIDENCE ONLY. The ratified grading ladder binds: an 1839 or 1840 appearance alone is never an 1835 resident, and 1840 household composition is never back-projected to the 1835-07-01 scene. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and an 1840 head is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

age_band.note: THE BAND THIS PERSON'S OWN BIRTH YEAR PUTS THEM IN on 1 July 1835. It is a view of a value already on this card and adds nothing to it; it exists so the age axis can be read across the whole layer at once, beside the bands the model draws for everybody else.

birth_year.note: A BIRTH INTERVAL OUT OF A MAN'S OWN STATEMENT OF HIS AGE. He registered at the Calumet Club's reception to the settlers of Chicago on 27 May 1879 and gave his age as 74: "Carpenter, Philo, | 1832, | Mass. | 74 | Chicago.". An age of 74 completed years given on that day means the birth falls after 27 May 1804 and on or before 27 May 1805, so the birth year is 1804 or 1805. The subtraction is this project's; the page states no year of birth. IT IS A RECOLLECTION, forty-four years after the scene date — better than a recollection about somebody else, and still not a record. The merge onto this person is the old-settler crosswalk's own (OS1), in data/research/old_settlers/people.json.

research_note: CHICAGO'S FIRST DRUGGIST, AND THE HOUSEHOLD THAT SHOWS WHY A RESIDENT CAN OUTLAST A BUILDING LINK. Carpenter is documented from July 1832 to the 1880s; which of his two shops he was standing in on 1 July 1835 is a structures question this project has already argued and not settled.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. WHAT THIS PASS RULED ONTO THIS HOUSEHOLD, named so the ruling can be found again: each volume below is followed by the printed entries it set against this person and the status the crosswalk ruled them at — a single entry carries what its own `could_carry` declares, and an ambiguous or contested match carries nothing and is shown so that the silence is legible. carpenter_philo, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 — f1839_e0242 (a single entry); carpenter_philo, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 — f1843_e0550 (a single entry); carpenter_philo, Norris's Chicago directory of 1844 — n1844_e0294 (a single entry).

address_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints this address against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Carpenter, Philo, druggist and apothecary, South Water st'. It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.

back_projection.note: NOT READ BACK, BECAUSE SOMETHING BETTER ALREADY STANDS. Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints an address against this name in 1839, and it is left where it is. An 1835 placement already stands: this household works at `carpenter_south_water_store`, and clause 2 says an attested 1835 placement always beats a door printed 4 years later. The later address stays on the record as 1839's evidence and moves nothing.
